meta.title: Who really said "If you want others to be happy, practice compassion"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to the Dalai Lama, and consistent with his teaching — but the earliest source we could trace is a 2000 anthology, not a work of his own.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you want others to be happy, practice compassion. If you want to be happy, practice compassion.'?
meta.ogDescription: Almost certainly the Dalai Lama — but no primary source. We show what the record actually supports.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: born 6 July 1935 · Tenzin Gyatso, 14th Dalai Lama; Tibetan Buddhist spiritual leader
answer.sourceLine: This is credited to the Dalai Lama everywhere it appears, and it restates a point he has made in public for decades — that compassion serves the person practising it as much as its object. What we could not find is a primary source: no book, speech or interview of his that we could reach contains the sentence. The earliest documented appearance is a daily-meditations anthology from 2000 that quotes him without saying where from.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Meditations for Living In Balance” by Anne Wilson Schaef (2000), p. 11
A daily-meditations anthology quoting him — not a work of his own

source.excerpt: If you want others to be happy, practice compassion. If you want to be happy, practice compassion.
trail: Wikiquote’s page for the 14th Dalai Lama ↗ carries the sentence and sources it precisely one step: “As quoted in Meditations for Living In Balance: Daily Solutions for People Who Do Too Much (2000) by Anne Wilson Schaef, p. 11.” An “as quoted in” citation is a report of a quotation, not a primary source.

We confirmed that the Schaef book exists as cited — the Internet Archive’s catalogue record ↗ gives the title, the author and the year 2000. We could not read its page 11: the scan is lending-restricted, so we are not claiming to have seen the sentence in it.

We also searched Quote Investigator, which has published no investigation of this line, so there is no specialist finding to defer to here — that is our own search result, not a claim we can cite. Many popular pages assign the quote to the 1998 book “The Art of Happiness” ↗, but every instance of that claim we found traces back to user-submitted quotation sites, and we could not verify it against the book.
The Dalai Lama’s date of birth, 6 July 1935, is confirmed against his Wikipedia entry ↗.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to show, because we could not find the sentence in any work by the Dalai Lama. What is reproduced here is the quotation as it is recorded on Wikiquote, which cites it as quoted in Anne Wilson Schaef’s 2000 anthology.
source.rightsHolder: His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama and his publishers
source.rightsNote: The Dalai Lama was born in 1935, so everything he has said or published falls far on the copyright side of the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff — whichever work first carried these words, they are in copyright. Because we could not identify that work, no edition is named here.

author.metaLine: born 6 July 1935 · Tenzin Gyatso, 14th Dalai Lama; Tibetan Buddhist leader and 1989 Nobel Peace laureate
author.bio: His Holiness Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama, was born to a farming family in Amdo in 1935 and recognised as the Dalai Lama as a small child. He has lived in exile in India since 1959, and spent the following decades arguing a consistent case: that compassion is not a religious ornament but a practical requirement for human societies, and that it can be cultivated with or without religion. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line works by repetition: the same instruction answers two different questions. Whether you set out to help other people or to feel better yourself, the prescribed action does not change — which is a compact way of saying that the division between the two is less real than it looks.

That is a recognisably Buddhist argument rather than a greetings-card sentiment, and it is one the Dalai Lama has made in plainer prose for years: compassion is not a sacrifice you make for others but the most reliable route to your own peace of mind.
detailsBody: A note on why this page says “attributed” rather than “verified.” We are confident the thought is his; what we cannot do is point to the book, speech or interview where he said it in these words. That gap matters, because quotation anthologies are exactly where polished paraphrases enter circulation looking like transcripts.

His Nobel acceptance speech of 1989 puts the same idea in the register he actually uses when speaking: “true happiness comes from a sense of inner peace and contentment, which in turn must be achieved through the cultivation of altruism, of love and compassion.” That sentence is sourced; the aphorism on this page, so far, is not.
context.pull: The same instruction answers both questions.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote records the quotation and sources it as quoted in Meditations for Living In Balance (2000) by Anne Wilson Schaef, p. 11 — a secondary anthology, not a work by the Dalai Lama.

Wikiquote’s transcriptions of the Dalai Lama’s 1989 Nobel acceptance speech include the sentence about true happiness coming from inner peace achieved through cultivating altruism, love and compassion.
The Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for Anne Wilson Schaef, Meditations for Living in Balance, dated 2000.
The 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, was born 6 July 1935 and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989.
